name: Sorghum
summary: How Filipino farmers grow sorghum for grain and animal feed, a crop known as batad among Maguindanao and Ilocano farmers that takes drought better than corn. It is grown much like corn in furrows, and the stubble can give a second crop.
season: Planted at the start of the rains, around May to June, or after the rice harvest in the dry season, around November to January, on the moisture left in the field. In Mindanao it is grown in both seasons.
material: Dry seed, bought or saved from the heads of the best plants of open pollinated types. The seed is small, so it is sown shallow and thinly. When drilled in rows, farmers use about 8 to 10 kg of seed a hectare.
spacing: Rows about 60 to 75 cm apart, with one plant every 10 to 15 cm after thinning.
water: Rainfed. Sorghum rides out dry spells better than corn, so it is often the crop planted on the leftover moisture after rice.
fertilizer: Complete fertilizer (14 14 14) in the furrow at planting and urea (46 0 0) at about four weeks before hilling up. Many farmers give it less fertilizer than corn, and the ratoon crop gets another side dressing of urea.
care: Off barring and hilling up with the plow, hand weeding of the rows, and thinning at two to three weeks. Bird scaring is the big chore once the grain starts to fill.
harvest: Grain sorghum is ready at about 100 to 115 days, when the grain is hard and the leaves below the head start drying. The heads are cut, sun dried and threshed. For silage, some growers cut the whole plant earlier while the grain is still soft.

steps.title: Plow the field
steps.how: Plow once when the soil is moist enough, with a carabao or a tractor.

steps.title: Harrow
steps.how: Harrow one or two times to get a fine seedbed and kill sprouting weeds. Small sorghum seed needs fine soil to come up well.

steps.title: Open the furrows
steps.how: Open shallow furrows about 60 to 75 cm apart.

steps.title: Fertilizer in the furrow
steps.how: Drop complete fertilizer (14 14 14) along the furrow and cover it with a little soil.

steps.title: Drill the seed
steps.how: Trickle the seed thinly along the furrow and cover it with only 2 to 3 cm of soil.

steps.title: Off barring and weeding
steps.how: Plow along the rows with the soil thrown away from the plants, then hand pull the weeds in the row. Young sorghum grows slowly and loses easily to weeds.

steps.title: Thin the plants
steps.how: Pull extra seedlings so one plant stands every 10 to 15 cm along the row.

steps.title: Watch the young plants
steps.how: Check the whorls for armyworm and the leaves for aphids, and pull out sickly plants.

steps.title: Side dress urea
steps.how: Drop urea (46 0 0) beside the plants on moist soil.

steps.title: Hill up
steps.how: Plow toward the rows to cover the fertilizer and pile soil at the base of the plants.

steps.title: Guard the heads from birds
steps.how: Birds go for the grain as it fills. Farmers chase them off in the morning and late afternoon, hang noisy cans and strips, and on small plots tie bags over the heads.

steps.title: Cut the heads
steps.how: Harvest at about 100 to 115 days, when the grains are hard and can no longer be dented with a thumbnail. Cut the heads with a sickle or a knife.

parts.title: Bite a grain
parts.how: From about a month after flowering, pinch or bite a few grains from the middle of the head. When they are hard and crack instead of squashing, the crop is ready. A dark spot where the grain joins the head is another sign.

parts.title: Cut with a long stem
parts.how: Cut each head with a sickle or knife about a foot below its base. The long stem makes the heads easy to bundle, hang and beat later.

parts.title: Harvest early if you will ratoon
parts.how: If you plan a second crop from the stubble, cut the heads a little sooner, at about 30 days after flowering. Plants left to overripen send up a poor ratoon.

steps.title: Dry and thresh
steps.how: Sun dry the heads for a few days, thresh by beating or with a thresher, then dry the grain again before storing.

parts.title: Sun dry the heads
parts.how: Lay the heads on canvas or a concrete floor in the full sun and turn them now and then. Sorghum is harder to thresh than palay, so the heads must be really dry first.

parts.title: Beat out the grain
parts.how: Put the dry heads in a sack or on a canvas and beat them with a stick, or feed them through a thresher, until the grain falls free.

parts.title: Winnow and dry again
parts.how: Winnow off the chaff and bits of head, then spread the grain in the sun once more until it is hard and dry enough to keep, about 14 percent moisture or less.

parts.title: Sack and store
parts.how: Pack the grain in clean sacks and pile them in an airy storeroom so the grain does not heat up. Keep seed for the next planting from the best heads of the best plants, apart from the rest.

steps.title: Ratoon the stubble
steps.how: Cut the old stalks close to the ground, weed and side dress, and the stubble sends up new shoots for a smaller second crop.

parts.title: Cut the stalks at ground level
parts.how: Within three days of harvesting the heads, cut every old stalk right at the ground. The best new shoots come from buds below the soil. Stalks cut high sprout weak, uneven shoots from every node that the wind easily breaks.

parts.title: Water right away
parts.how: Irrigate the field as soon as the stalks are cut. Cut stubble will not sprout without water.

parts.title: Fertilize at once
parts.how: Spread the whole fertilizer dose for the regrowth as soon as the stalks are cut, because it ripens about 10 to 15 days ahead of the first crop.

parts.title: Weed and watch it like the first crop
parts.how: Keep the weeds down with shallow cultivation and spot hand weeding, and watch for the same pests and birds as in the first crop.

mistakes: Sowing the small seed too deep, so few seedlings come up.
Not thinning, so crowded plants give small heads.
Letting weeds take over in the first month, when young sorghum grows slowly.
Leaving the ripening heads unguarded, so birds eat a big part of the harvest.
Storing grain before it is fully dry.
better: Use a variety or hybrid suited to your purpose, grain or silage, and your season.
Prepare a fine seedbed, sow shallow and thin early to an even stand.
Feed by a soil test and split the nitrogen between planting and four weeks.
Plant with neighbors at the same time so bird pressure is shared.
Ratoon only a healthy first crop and feed the ratoon with urea.

watering.traditional: Sorghum is grown on rain alone. Farmers plant it at the start of the rains or after the rice harvest on the moisture left in the field, because it rides out dry spells better than corn.
watering.method: Rain only on most farms. Where water is close, a furrow watering from a pump or canal, in the morning or late afternoon.
watering.rainfed: This is the usual way. Plant at the start of the rains, or soon after the rice harvest while the field is still wet, so flowering comes before the soil dries out. Keep the field weed free so the weeds do not take the moisture.
watering.dryseason: A crop sown after rice usually needs no watering. In a very dry year, one furrow watering at booting or flowering pays back the most grain.
watering.wet: Sorghum stands short floods better than corn but not water that stays for days. Keep the furrow ends open, and harvest the heads before long rains mold the grain.

schedule.often: Plant into moist soil. If you have water and the soil is dry, wet the furrows once before planting
schedule.amount: Enough to moisten the seed row, with no water left standing
schedule.why: The small seed sown shallow dries out fast in dry soil.
Young sorghum stands dry spells and grows deep roots.

schedule.often: Water only in a long dry spell, after the side dressing if the soil is dry
schedule.amount: One furrow watering that soaks in
schedule.why: The urea works only in moist soil.

schedule.often: If water is at hand and the soil is dry, water once
schedule.why: Drought when the head comes out gives heads with few grains.

schedule.often: Water once more in a hard drought
schedule.why: Moist soil fills the grain heavy.

schedule.often: Water right after cutting the stalks for a ratoon, if the soil is dry
schedule.amount: A furrow watering along the stubble
schedule.why: Moisture helps the stubble send up even new shoots.

critical: Booting and flowering, about day 60 to 80: the soil must not be bone dry, or the heads fill poorly.
Right after cutting for a ratoon: the stubble needs moisture to shoot again.

signs.dry: Leaves roll up tight and turn gray green, growth stops, and the heads come out late or stay partly inside the leaf.
signs.wet: Yellow lower leaves, stunted plants in the low spots, and moldy heads after long rain.

better: If you can water only once, water at booting or flowering.
Water the stubble right after cutting if you want a good ratoon crop.
